transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-08 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees (Redwood): Maya Chen, Liam O'Neill, Priya Rao
Attendees (BrightCart): Ethan Park, Sofia Martinez, Oliver Lee, Jenna

Auto-summary: quick sandbox demo and resiliency patterns for hosted streaming generation.

[00:00:05] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya, I'm the AE on this account, with me is Liam, our senior systems engineer, and Priya from docs. how's the audio on your side?
[00:00:14] Ethan: good to go, thanks. excited to see the hosted gen flow, we want to replace our current webhook-based chat with something lower latency.
[00:00:21] Maya: awesome, quick agenda: we'll show the hosted generation sandbox, demonstrate streaming chunks, then go into parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), and finish with recommended retry and idempotency strategies. plenty of time for Q&A.
[00:00:35] Sofia: just so you know, our main constraints are 95th percentile latency under 300ms for quick answers, and cost per session under $0.05. also must be SOC2-compliant for user data.
[00:00:48] Liam: got it. we usually balance that with batching and prefix caching; in hosted mode you get KV cache benefits automatically for repeated contexts, but we can discuss dedicated options if you need lower tail latency.
[00:01:05] Oliver: quick question — we run on GCP, does your hosted product support region pinning?
[00:01:10] Maya: yes, we have regional endpoints and smart routing; we'll provision the sandbox in GCP-US for these tests.
[00:01:17] Jenna: and about data retention — do you keep logs? we need audit logs turned on.
[00:01:22] Liam: by default we keep ephemeral logs for debugging, but for enterprise customers we offer longer retention and audit logs via the console and can integrate with your SIEM. we'll share the SOC2 and retention FAQ after.

[00:02:00] Demo start / Console tour
[00:02:05] Liam: ok switching screens — this is the sandbox org. first, create a key, then open the Generations playground. I'm going to paste a short chat prompt: "You are BrightCart shopping assistant. Greet and ask for product name." Selecting streaming mode now, you'll see partial tokens arrive.
[00:02:30] (screen noises)
[00:02:35] Liam: here we go — the UI shows a stream of delta events, each chunk includes tokens and an approximate delta T. note that streaming uses chunked output, you will get multiple events per response.
[00:02:50] Sofia: is each chunk retriable or do we need to request the whole message again?
[00:02:55] Liam: good point. streaming is just delivery; if a connection drops mid-stream we recommend clients implement resumption or idempotent retries. typically you use an idempotency token per request so the service can deduplicate. if you re-send with the same token within the TTL, we return the final completed generation or a cached partial depending on settings.
[00:03:18] Ethan: what's the TTL for idempotency?
[00:03:21] Liam: default is 5 minutes in hosted, configurable for enterprise. also there is a request-level header for idempotency-key. we'll include example code.

[00:04:10] Parameters and cost discussion
[00:04:12] Maya: let's walk parameters. temp and top_p tune creativity; max_tokens caps output length. also presence_penalty and stop sequences matter for chat flows. shorter max_tokens and stricter stop sequences = lower token cost and faster streams.
[00:04:30] Sofia: we usually keep temperature 0.2 for product recommender to avoid hallucinations. what's your recommendation?
[00:04:36] Liam: 0.0-0.3 for deterministic assistant is typical. for safety and consistency reduce top_p as well. we recommend running a small eval set — Redwood Optimize can suggest parameter sweeps based on your metrics.
[00:04:50] Maya: and when you need to lower cost we can suggest quantized model variants or cache strategies. hosted endpoints will automatically route to cheaper variants when appropriate unless you pin a model.

[00:05:30] Retry strategies deep dive
[00:05:35] Liam: now retries — common failure modes: transient capacity errors, network timeouts, and server-side tokenization hiccups. general playbook: exponential backoff with jitter, max 3 retries for idempotent requests, and don't retry non-idempotent ones. for streaming, if the connection fails after partial chunks, client should attempt to re-open with same idempotency token and ask for final result.
[00:06:05] Ethan: do you provide a client SDK that encapsulates this behavior?
[00:06:09] Liam: yes, we have SDKs in Node/Python that include a retry middleware and streaming helpers that resume or re-request with idempotency-key built-in. they also expose hooks to reconsume KV cache to avoid repeating full context resends.
[00:06:25] Sofia: curious about exactly how resume works. if the model produced 60 tokens, and we received 30, and connection drops — how do we avoid duplication?
[00:06:33] Liam: good question; our approach is server-side chunk checkpoints. when you reconnect with same idempotency token you can pass last_received_token_index and the server will continue or return the final completed response depending on whether generation completed. caveat: for strict low-latency cases this can add small overhead; for determinism we recommend full-request idempotency and dedup on client as well.
[00:06:56] Jenna: is there any extra cost for resume?
[00:07:00] Maya: you may re-charge for tokens generated the first time unless the server served from cache — we try to avoid double-billing via dedup logic, but it's a nuanced topic; we'll include billing examples.

[00:08:20] Live SDK snippet (Node)
[00:08:23] Liam: pasting a quick Node snippet: create client, send generation with idempotencyKey, enable streaming handler: onDelta -> render; onClose -> check finalStatus. (snippets shown in chat).
[00:08:45] (typing)
[00:08:50] Sofia: can you paste the retry backoff function?
[00:08:53] Liam: yep — exponential with base 200ms, factor 2, jitter 50-150ms, max attempts 3. code's on the repo link.

[00:10:10] Latency tuning and batching tradeoffs
[00:10:13] Liam: batching increases throughput but adds queuing latency; for your use-case (interactive shopping chat) we recommend small batch sizes or continuous batching with short cutoffs. in hosted we can configure burst lanes for low latency but predictable throughput.
[00:10:31] Ethan: any guidance on model selection — we care about concise answers, not long-form creative text.
[00:10:37] Maya: pick a base chat model tuned for instruction following and low token spend; we can recommend a trimmed variant. we also have quantized variants for cost savings. Redwood Optimize can run a cost/quality sweep and provide a recommended model profile.

[00:12:05] Security and compliance questions
[00:12:07] Ethan: SOC2 is a must, SSO and SCIM for user provisioning, and KMS integration for keys.
[00:12:12] Liam: we support SAML SSO, SCIM, and KMS integrations for private deployments; for hosted there are managed keys, and enterprise customers can use customer-managed keys in many cases. also audit logs and RBAC are available in the console.
[00:12:30] Sofia: do you support VPC/VPN for private peering?
[00:12:33] Maya: for Private deployment yes; hosted supports private connectivity options (VPC peering) for enterprise customers. we'll include network diagrams in the follow-up.

[00:14:00] Q&A and edge cases
[00:14:05] Oliver: what happens if the streaming connection is slow and emits very small chunks? will that increase cost?
[00:14:11] Liam: cost is per-token regardless of chunk size; however, many small chunks may increase round-trip overhead. the runtime aggregates tokens into chunks server-side, but client-side rendering can affect perceived latency. tune chunk thresholds in SDK if needed.
[00:14:28] Jenna: and rate limits? we expect bursts during sales events.
[00:14:32] Maya: sandbox has generous limits; production you can request quota increases or use Dedicated reserved capacity for bursty workloads with guaranteed lanes.

[00:16:00] Live scenario: product recommendation microflow
[00:16:05] Liam: let's demo a quick end-to-end: user query -> prebuilt prompt template -> send to hosted generations streaming -> assemble partials in UI -> final confirmation + upsert session cache. showing rapid 1-2 chunk response for short answers.
[00:16:40] (demo voiceover)
[00:17:05] Sofia: that looked pretty snappy, what's the 95th p for that demo?
[00:17:10] Liam: in the sandbox with default routing we see ~220ms 95th for that short prompt size; your mileage may vary based on region and model.

[00:18:00] Troubleshooting tips
[00:18:03] Maya: if you see increased tail latency check: model size selection, batching behavior, prefix cache hit-rate, and network egress. enable tracing to see per-token latencies in console.
[00:18:20] Ethan: if we run tests and see spikes what level of support do we get?
[00:18:25] Maya: enterprise support with SLAs is available; for early POC we'll assign an SE and a CSM.

[00:20:00] Billing nuance recap
[00:20:03] Liam: billing is per-token; retries may or may not double-charge depending on whether the server recognized idempotency and served from cache. we will attach billing examples; for high-volume flows we recommend model profiling and Optimize suggestions.

[00:22:30] Customer concerns — latency vs cost decision framework
[00:22:35] Sofia: we need a simple rule to present to finance: when do we pick cheaper model vs when do we pay for lower latency?
[00:22:40] Maya: rule of thumb: for short hard-latency answers pick smaller, faster models with reserved burst lanes; for complex completions use larger models. Redwood Optimize can provide the expected cost per QPS curve so finance can decide.

[00:24:00] Live notes: sharing artifacts
[00:24:03] Maya: I'll share the sandbox invite, the example repo, and a short demo video. Liam will share the retry playbook and a docs link to idempotency and streaming behavior.
[00:24:20] Priya: docs link: https://docs.redwood.ai/streaming-playbook (note: link may be redacted in recording)

[00:25:00] Wrap and next steps
[00:25:02] Maya: quick recap: we'll provision sandbox, BrightCart will run 500-message benchmark, and we'll reconvene to review numbers. any blockers?
[00:25:12] Ethan: none from our side. please include SOC2 and retention details in follow-up.
[00:25:20] Jenna: one more — do you have a recommended schema for passing session state and conversation ids?
[00:25:25] Liam: yes, we'll send a sample session schema in the repo; short answer: include conversation_id, message_index, and idempotency_key per request.

[00:26:00] Closing chatter and light cross-talk
[00:26:05] (unintelligible)
[00:26:20] Sofia: thanks, see you all next week.
[00:26:24] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with links and invite. bye.
